title: Memory hierarchy and caches
kicker: ENCT 303 · Computer Organization and Architecture · Chapter 4
subtitle: Fast memory is small, big memory is slow — a cache makes the big slow one look fast by remembering what you just used.

sections.title: The hierarchy
sections.body: No memory is fast, large and cheap at once, so computers stack them: registers (sub-ns, bytes), cache (ns, KB–MB), main memory (≈100 ns, GB), disk/SSD (µs–ms, TB). It works because of locality: temporal (what you used you will use again) and spatial (what is near what you used will be used). The hierarchy moves data in blocks so neighbours come along.

questions.prompt: Looping over an array element by element is fast on a cache mainly because of…

choices.text: Spatial locality — one block fetch brings in the next few elements too.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Each element is used once in the pass.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each miss loads a whole block, so the following accesses hit.

sections.title: Mapping: where may a block go?
sections.body:
A block of memory can be placed in: exactly one line (direct-mapped: cheap, but blocks that map to the same line keep evicting each other — conflict misses); any line (fully associative: flexible, expensive to search); or any line within one set (set-associative, e.g. 2-way: the usual compromise). An address splits into tag | index | offset; the index picks the set, the tag is compared with each line in it, the offset picks the byte.

Same 5 addresses 0 8 0 6 8 into a 4-line cache: direct-mapped gets 5 misses, 2-way 4, fully associative 3.

worked.why: A 32-bit address, 4 KB direct-mapped cache with 16-byte blocks. Offset bits = log₂16 = 4.

questions.prompt: Why does the direct-mapped cache miss on the second reference to address 0?

choices.text: The cache is too small for any data.
Address 8 mapped to the same line and evicted it (a conflict miss).

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: It has four lines and only three distinct blocks.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: With one allowed place, two hot blocks that share an index thrash.

responses.body: It was loaded by the first reference.

sections.title: Replacement and write policies
sections.body: When a set is full, replacement picks a victim: LRU (least recently used), FIFO, or random. On a write: write-through updates memory every time (simple, slow; often with a write buffer); write-back marks the line dirty and writes memory only on eviction (fast; complicated). On a write miss: write-allocate loads the block first, no-write-allocate writes straight to memory.

questions.prompt: What does a write-back cache save compared with write-through?

choices.text: Memory traffic: repeated writes to one line cost one write at eviction.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The dirty bit remembers that memory is stale.

sections.title: Average memory access time
sections.body: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. With a 1-cycle hit, 100-cycle penalty and the fully associative run above (40% hits) AMAT is 61 cycles — a cache with a 90% hit rate would give 1 + 0.1 × 100 = 11. Multi-level caches nest the formula: the L1 miss penalty is the L2 access time.

questions.prompt: Hit time 2 ns, miss rate 5%, miss penalty 80 ns. AMAT?

figures.caption: Figure 4.4.1 — AMAT of the fully associative run
figures.note: The AMAT appears in the results.

problems.prompt: Direct-mapped, 64 KB cache, 32-byte blocks, 32-bit addresses. Give the tag, index and offset widths.
problems.answer: Offset = 5 bits (32 B). Lines = 64K/32 = 2048 → index = 11. Tag = 32 − 11 − 5 = 16 bits.

sections.title: Semiconductor and external memory
sections.body: SRAM (flip-flops) is fast and used for caches; DRAM (a capacitor plus transistor, refreshed constantly) is denser and used for main memory, in DDR DIMM/SODIMM modules. ROM/flash hold firmware. Externally: magnetic disk, SSD, optical and tape; RAID levels 1–5 add redundancy (see the OS course for a worked RAID 5 parity example).

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Locality makes a small fast memory effective.
  • Direct, set-associative and fully associative trade cost against conflict misses.
  • AMAT = hit + miss rate × penalty.
